text.p: 1 Sunday night 1708/9

Dear William , I have never been tolerably well since my Tanfield journey, but I don't attribute my indisposition which is more than ordnary to that, but to the violence of the weather, which falls att present, and is to come down. This obliges me to request you to add to former favours that of representing me at the Coal Office to morrow, where the Mayor's case is to be debated. I will if he reckons a favour allow him not exceeding 70 tens, to be taken off when we have no throng and no otherwise. On this account you may allege that in case of necessary mixtures from others, the Office must spare us as much as they can etc., which I leave to you. If Tom Allen be taken in, the salary must not be near so great as formerly mentioned. These and all other things I leave to your discretion, who can manage much better than, kind friend, yours in reality, H. L.
2 Wedensday afternoon 1708/9

Honest William , I enclosed you last Monday my father's by John Watson which I hope you have answered in those parts which I could say nothing too. I have received 17 dozen of bottles, part of the hogshead of lost clarett; your cooper tells Hugh Ridley there remains but 5 odd bottles. I am afraid that man abuses both you and me. The wine is hugely improved so that it would vex me to loose att least 3 dozen . I have att last got Joseph Blaky's computation of profitt for Bensham colliery next year which amounts to £117 and no more. This I believe is true. He computes 770 delivering tens to be wrought att Bensham out of which this £117 profitt will arise,
with 100 tens pan coal. The other 400 tens are to be wrought out of Whitefield but I am against that, choosing rather to lye in that part and receive off the Office £400 compensation for as many tens, provided Mr Rogers will agree to it. It is I am sure his interest as well as that of the Office. I am sorry you could not conclude att your last meeting. Herin enclose for your perusal my uncle's which you will return, and when you see Poyen acquaint him with the contents. My legs are so inflamed since my last journey that I am extremely uneasy; the last night I never slept till 5 in the morning and then very disturbed. I have not bin so much out of order a great while, which obliges me to rules and avoiding company. I am ...
3 July 29th 1710

Dear friend, on Wednesday 7 night in the evening I was taken with a shivering cold fit, which obliged me to hasten to a warm bed. I added a blankett to my number, but after 1 1/2 hours sleep I wakened in a fire, which lasted all that night. The next day I was invited to be bearer to my cousin Thomas Liddell's mother in law, but finding my illness increase, sent back my tickett, and desired they would pitch upon another. In short they had no time to provide, so it fell to Signor's lot to supply my place. The doctor pronounces me in a strong feavor; this confined me 6 days to bed and has so weakened me, and my head is so light that I can scarce use a pen, further than to tell you I had your last. Lord President Somers is perfectly well apprised of our case. Lord Chancellor Cowper has bin dangerously ill of the strangury for many days, and is this day gon into the country for a little relief from business, as well as benefit of air. As to the overstocking the river with coal, that is a danger that may divide us among our selves; but as soon as the keelmen are got again quietly to work, then will be the time to lessen production when no apprehension can be of their joining another strike . By the Captain I perceive we have but 3 ship coal pits going, and that is but what the worst of years will carry off. You will consider well before you lower, and not to do it unless of utmost necessity. You have not sent the paper of Sunderland's coal price to the Master,
and the comparison with ours. You may depend there was (upon the hearing att Council) an order given for one regiment or more to be sent to the town's assistance. Your method of treating with Captain Scott was perfectly right, and much more may be compass't with fair than foul means. We shall hear by to morrow's post how they fettled to their work. We hang an arse yet as to the purchase. Money indeed is very hard to be come by, and times ticklish. Nothing can be don with the Towlers while David Dixon is concerned. Indeed I can't advise your going much further than £30 a year for Jimmy Clavering's expenses least as Lady Ann says the whole should be scrupled, but for this present year he is att liberty to bring in as he pleases. I hope Trumball will stand steady to you; I find George Vane does not care for renewing his lease with Lord Widdrington since the sisters will first be paid their demands out of the coal mine. There is no prospect of my coming into the country shortly, att soonest will be next spring. Let your age be what it will, your aptness to business will not I dare say fail you. It should not att least till you have bred up a good apprentice. A dissolution is talked off as if to be next September . This balks my father's fancy chiefly as to the 2 manors. I have communicated your opinion of this matter to her, and she is perfectly for it, and hath spoke off it ofter than once. I have wrote till my head is running round, so am obliged to drop my pen, and hasten to bed, which is the only place that is fit for me. I am with all sincerity in all circumstances, your most affectionate friend, Governor .
4 August 15th 1710

Kind friend, I have yours of the 8th and 10th are with me. Am sorry no better success attended your own trial, though the fine was very inconsiderable. However you have this happiness of being reconciled to the lady, whose favour you don't a little value for the sake of her husband. The spiriting away of a jury man is a practice I never so much as heard of before. My father had most of your letters during my illness and answered them. As to the contents I then gave him my opinion as well as I could so that discoursing him upon those heads will I believe be sufficient . No wonder that endeavours should be used to present the Contractors; we have friends enough in your town to putt the judge upon such a project, had he no orders from court. I am and always was of opinion that a bank of £500 should be raised and kept for extraordinary uses. I proposed it before I came out of the country but no notice was taken of it. Nay when I came to town I mentioned it to young Wortley who seemed to approve. I can't imagine the reason why the last year's groats are not yet collected. Are they afraid of trusting it? Sure a safe hand might be found out to lodge it in. Indeed I apprehend as I formerly wrote and of late to Mr Poyen, that the consequences of not keeping touch with the dealers would prove very dangerous and occasion such a confusion as would
shake the agreement more than all other artifices that our enemies could practice. I design for the Gate to morrow to see if I can stop their mouths by fair promises, but I doubt I shall not succeed since they are a sort of people that will not be fed with words only. It is worth the consideration of the Five and that speedily too, therefore I desire you will earnestly recommend that matter to them. I think you have assessed Jimmy's allowance very moderately and what no body can object against. Certain it is that now he must be att a greater expense, considering the disposition of the trade, and this I have not failed inculcate when ever had a proper opportunity. My feavor hangs still upon me and preys upon my spirits. I don't indulge it for I go abroad 3 hours every day into the air. I have no news to send you. I am entirely ...
To Mr. William Cotesworth, to be sent by the postmaster of Durham.
5 London October 28th 1710

You were resolved not to putt me to a sixpenny charge whilst att Bath, but you might be assured I should not have scrupled any for such favours from you. I am now safe returned but in no better plight of health than when I went; I have a continued cold pain that settles about my kidneys and
allows me no rest night or day, but especially against change of weather it is not to be bore. This induces me readily to comply with any prescription, be it never so troublesome; and God knows if ever I shall see the end. I must submit though the burden be never so great. I was extremely concerned at poor William Heslop's? death; the loss was great to the public and no less to the private concerns of his family. Pray how doe you hear he has left matters? I have seen a letter to Signor which gives but a melancholy account. Whatever you write shall be kept secret. In relation to trade, I am vexed you should have so great a stock a fore hand of a commodity that will grow so much worse by lying and not a little concerned to hear from you that the Moorgate seam should prove so ordinary. I must confess I suspected that all the new pickings would prove such for they were formerly left by some extraordinary extremities, such as dykes, and there I am sure the coal can't be good. Both masters, dealors, and consumers exclaim heavily and will not on any terms touch them. I wrote last post my sentiments to Jimmy to be communicated to you and wish for your improvement on them. No private advance of praemium will doe if the coal will not in it self answer the markett. As the year went I doubted not your meeting with considerable rubs in your own private vend, yet all things considered you are come off with neighbour fare, and what by experience you find amiss in this year's proceeding you will mend in the next. You will continue to keep dunning the salt owners that are in arrear; they will bear it and doe expect it. As the demand is great for salt, they will be in time enabled to give you a large supply. One would be apt to think now that carriage is laid off and the pans like to go till Christmas, that those sort of coals should naturally advance in price, but that you can best judge off. Charles Sanderson is transacting what he thinks necessary in relation to the manors. I see him 2 days ago and tells me that he now doubts if £6000 will carry them. I think it is the full price or rather more considering that since the last bidding, part of the lease's term is expiring. On another hand the ticklishness of the times ought to be weighed as also the indifferent title to Nusam estate. Manlove talks of raising to some thousands more than the above mentioned sum. Your thoughts pray on these several heads. I am in trouble about poor Jimmy Nicholson's bad success and that he should loose it by so great
a majority. Did his friends stand true to him to the last? For your part I know how much you value the censure of the church . Pray what is become of Daniell? I have not heard from him almost these 3 months and though I wrote to him from Bath, yet it produced nothing but silence. Pray give me a particular account of your election when over. I shall long to know how it has gon and how the generality of the magistrates managed on that occasion. Here are no times for news. P.S. Att long run I have received a letter from Daniell with the enclosed vend of the river till the 30th September last. Shortly will be sent down the late order in Chancery for working Whitefield. You will remark that we are to keep the account of disbursments and neat produce of that colliery distinct from all others. You will consider if it would not be proper that Mr Barns should write to Mr Cole that he can procure his lord a tenant for what remains of Hedley Fell, and that if not accepted of now it must lye for ever, by reason our branch from Chopwell must shortly be pulled up, after we have got the small quantity of coals and lead taken away. I wish twixt this and Christmas you would when at leisure draw out an account of moneys received and the produce of any of the collieries. My head is very giddy and warns me to conclude being with sincerity ...
8 December 4th 1710

Since my last to you I have seen Charles Sanderson, who tells me that Mr Manlove's goldsmith has bid £7000 for the manors etc. but is backward in filing the report; that Jackson designs to move the court to oblige him to file it and pay part of his money as usual in those cases. This goldsmith, the person that has bid, is a man of little or no substance and Charles thinks that he will be obliged to drop it att last. Nay in all probability your friends may take the bargain off his hands in case they approve of it, for he will never be able to go through with it, and before all parties be brought to consent (which must be first obtained) much time will be spent, att least a twelve-month. So that if you have any thoughts, if you will either write to me or Charles (but he will be the properest to satisfy any scruples or clear objections) he promises to doe all the service he is capable off. The sum that is generally paid into court on this and the like occasions is about £400 or £500 in the nature of earnest and to satisfy the court that the party dos design to proceed. The two objections you raised in your last are the chief that can affect the contractors. I showed my uncle your letter, but as he was going out of town we had not an opportunity of seeing the original. When that is don I shall press a resolution and I believe it will be thought convenient to cancel it, for in effect if the dealors should make a breach I don't see that the owners ever durst venture to sue their
covenant, least it be thought an illegal one and then it turns upon themselves. If the parties could be brought to lessen their numbers of waggons as also their winter works, it would effectually remedy the complaints under which the trade groaned this last year and this may be don without any exception. The abatement of keels will likewise contribute to make matters go more glibly in several respects. It is to be hoped that by your prudent management below, the keelmen will be brought to reason and see what is their true interest, which I take to be the joining in with their owners and endeavouring to serve their interests with zeal. Had you any discourse with Daniel Defoe when in the country? What sort off spirit possesses that man, who seems by the print of which he is suspected to be the author to encourage modestly speaking a refractoriness among that sort of people? Pray will you putt the Gentlemen in mind of providing against the evil day by remitting a convenient sum to be lodged in any hand they think fit. The sooner this is don the better for we don't know how soon we may be attacked. Be pleased to acquaint the Captain that the bill of forty pounds he returned me before I went to Bath from Starkin is not yet paid; the person on whom it is drawn has but twenty pounds of the master's in his hands and will not disburse a farthing for him. Let the Captain discourse Starkin about it. I mentioned thus much to him some posts ago but now the party is positive he will pay no more than he has effects for, which is as above. I am heartily glad John Johnson is like to doe well again. This rainy weather accompanied with storms of wind little inferior to the great one has much disturbed my corporation.

P.S. December 5th. Last night I had one from you and another from the Captain who tells me he has spoke to Starkin. Wortley is not yet come to town but I must tell you unless that money for the management be not remitted speedily, I believe you will find the two gentlemen very backward in pursuing the cause. Pray therefore press a supply without loss of time. I shall acquaint Mrs Clavering that you design to furnish the markett with choice coals this next year. I heartily rejoice that you have defeated Sir John Clavering etc. but am concerned poor Marly should be dismissed, since his crime can be no other than an intimacy with Ravensworth . If any post
should offer that may be fit for him, you will have him in view. Adieu I am in hast ... I should be glad of your tittle tattle; it would entertain us extremely att a time when public news is not so grateful.
12 December 23th 1710

In answer to yours by yesterday's post, you have fully satisfied us, so that we shall give Bowman liberty to provide for himself and we must depend upon our own and Clavering Stella fitters to help off with Bensham coals; and if any further assistance be needful, the Chamber must lend it when required. It must have bin the largeness off measure that contributed to the greatness of his vend, more than his management att the Gate. As the coal fleet is now arrived in the river and the weather very open, I believe the price of coals will not exceed 30s the best, which is no great encouragement . And in all probability there is more stock than will serve the consumption, especially since Candlemas, the time of your north countreymen's fitting out their ships draws near, so that I do apprehend that though next year's trade may be pretty brisk in the main, yet not very encouraging to the masters. Wherefore unless Enoch Hudson's coals be good in nature, round and in no great quantity, I would not advise your meddling with them on
any score, for you may depend on it, unless the commodity be choice in the above mentioned respects, you will never be able to make an interest att the Gate that will carry them off. They may indeed promise you and will expect performance from you, but you are to hope for little from them. My father is sorry he can't oblige Mr Rogers in the acceptance of his recommendation, he being engaged elsewhere several weeks ago, as I wrote word to George Bows, who had joined with his brother the Doctor in behalf of a friend of theirs about 3 weeks ago. Had Mr Rogers spoke early enough, I am sure my father has that regard for him as that he would not have failed of obliging him, but as matters are att present he can't possibly disengage. This you will be so kind as to acquaint that gentleman with, and at the same time make a tender of our humble services to him.

I thought Lord Barnard was so much pleased with your country air, which was so agreeable to his constitution, that he would not have entertained such sudden thoughts of quitting it, but his reasons are best known to himself. The offer indeed may be advantageous to Frank Baker but may not be of any long continuance; besides he must consider that the times are more likely to grow worse upon our hands rather than better, and consequently where there is little or no trade stirring the rents will infallibly fall. He has however this advantage of succeeding a landlord that gave little quarter to tenants, so that let him be never so strict and sharp upon them, it can be no reflection upon him. Doubtless he and his friends will weigh all circumstances before he engages. As to Bensham my father desires Mr Rogers would appoint a proper person and the Captain another to take a view of her jointly; after which by both their consents let them make cousin Baker their offers off keeping the way and waggons and inspecting the workings, and if possible letting to him the drawing off the water either by the day, so many shifts of horses, or by the great (for I doe suppose the quantity of water is now pretty much att a certainty). Pray what ever be don let Mr Rogers' concurrence be had and use your own discretions, to which my father leaves matters. You upon the spott must be the best judges, therefore it is referred to you to act in every respect. As to our Team waggon way you know we have improved it much within these 3 years last past, by raising the
ground where necessary and by easing of the runs as much as the situation of the ground would admit off. I remember about that time William Row offered to keep her for 14s a tenn, but when I came to discourse him about a conclusion he flew off it; however doe you and the Captain talk this matter with cousin Baker and see if you can article with him. I think this proposal a reasonable one: to keep the way and waggons etc. in repair att 10s a tenn in the low ground, that I call from the waggon bridge as far as the ditch which is above the engines, and all beyond that att 15s. I think with Frank's good management he may save handsomely by the year. We shall not stand with him for trifles, and shall not lead but in cases of necessity when the weather is indifferent. The Captain and you have the same power of concluding but it ought to be on that foundation, high ground and low a different price. We generally lead 1200 tens a year. I need not enlarge, you may guess our meaning. The fitters have taken the properest measures with the keelmen from whence I can't but expect the desired success, and as you intimate, it is much better that the owners don't appear in it; there seems to be no occasion for it. How will the town of Whitehaven be ever able to retrieve that prodigious loss in shipping? It is a vast sum for a place that was in a manner but falling into a trade that was considerable. I can't imagine why your magistrates should not have thought fit to have made an earlier publication of their being free from that infection; had it bin att another time of the year, their town might have suffered considerably by their backwardness. When does Mr Carr leave you? Were I in his circumstances I should not think it worth my while to spend so much time in a place where I had bin so indifferently treated. I perceive you made Surtis decamp in hast from the coffee house; was it not time when he found himself attack't in front and rear? Now good friend of mine do you and the Captain hasten to make the above mentioned bargains; you have full power and act as you both judge meet. I wish you success in that and all your undertakings and a merry Christmas, and remain ... P.S. My father is generally every other day extremely out of order. Thise frequent returns must of necessity spend nature. The doctor however gives hopes of relief as soon as the sun gets a little force. God grant him success.

TEI.text:
15 January 11th 1710/1
This must answer both yours of the 5th and that by yesterday's post. Since you only mention a projected design of electing the Mayor into the government of our company, I conclude the old one was continued and the exchange of Swaddell for Johnson is much more to my relish than it was before. I all along was of opinion that Fieldhouse would fall to Fenwick's share, and the lady Carr is beholden to you for keeping up her price. But as the benefactor is unknown to her, she will be att a loss how to return the obligation, though were she privy to it yet am apt to believe she would tread in her husband's steps and reward for your good deeds as he formerly has don. I hope the Regulation will not suffer much by the alderman going into another service; they will spare an extravagant salary by it. I find you are like to be the chief sufferer, by parting with the fitter you proposed to have had, but in my thoughts they ought to consider some method of assisting you in your vend att a reasonable price by way of acknowledgement for your good
services. With most people you know it is customary to christen their own child first, and as the world goes I don't see why you should not practice that rule. You would doe well to write to some of your correspondents to treat about an interest att the Gate without loss of time. I may assure you that till matters be settled for this last year's praemium I can't pretend to discourse them about Clavering Stella. It is to be owned that coals from several steaths have bin sent so very bad that it laid them under great difficulties; however I tell them they might have kept the prices more upon an equality if they would have exerted themselves, let their pretences to the contrary be never such. After all, it is worth the Gentleman's while to consider if the Contract can be upheld if these people be not gratified. Can their opposition distress us? I am of opinion they can, and even to a degree bring us into confusion and a breaking among our selves, by giving an extravagant preference in price to one or two concerns. We must consider that we sell for 11s, that is about 9s 4d neat, and it can't be imagined this price can be upheld but by our unanimous agreement among ourselves and a friendly correspondence with those necessary evils att the Gate. This ought to be well weighed and an answer must be given the dealors without loss of time. Twixt you and me, they told me that Mr Montagu's agent had promised that his share should be paid them though others did not. Don't take direct notice of this but by way of supposition the question may be put. I think the dealors in strictness merit a - but the only quaery is if we can subsist and keep together without their assistance.
My father approves in everything of what you have wrote concerning the future management of Bensham and has signified as much to the Captain by this post, whom he desires you will assist with your advice. He thinks Joseph Clark may as well be left out and be no undertaker but may be made useful as a check upon them. More needs not on this head, he having wrote word formerly that Grayson would be better outed than continue, but it must be don with as good a grace as can be. Now about the 2 manors. Mr Sanderson was here and designs to write to you shortly; in the mean time am to acquaint you that this very day Mr Gibson bid anew £5000 for them and the freehold and pressed to be reported the best bidder. Your agent offered £4000 for the manors and Mr Manlove att the same time £1500 for the freehold. An
argument arose for not separating the purchase, but it was carried that they might go to the best purchaser either by the lump or distinctly. Then it was pressed to have part of the money paid into court which was agreed to and time given till this day 3 weeks for making the report. Charles would be glad to know the utmost you would go and he will menage as warily as he can; there will be bidding one above another to be sure till the very day of report, so that you may send him full instructions. He thinks £200 or 300 ought to be returned him in case he be approved the best purchaser, to deposit in court. And as we agree that Mr Willson's name would be the properest to be made use off, he must be wrote to by the Alderman to desire him to send an order under his hand authorizing Charles
or the attorney Charles thinks fit to employ in his behalf to act for him. You will hear further particulars shortly to which I referr and am ...

text.p: 19 February 8th 1710/1

By last post you would have mine att large in answer I think to all former particulars as far as I could. Have since made further inquiry of some Members about the taking place of the additional duty on candles, but they tell me that the bill is not yet brought into the House and when it is a blank is left for the time. However one has promised me to ask Mr Lownds that
question and if he will resolve I shall know it and then you may depend it shall be communicated. I referred you to Charles for particulars of the business in his hands; I think it remains as when he wrote, Mr Wilson the best bidder att £6400. As there will be occasion to advance att least a brace of hundred pounds in court and money being very difficult to be had, my father has promised to go to his goldsmith, examine his cash and if he finds sufficient will advance for the present; but care must be taken to remitt it him speedily, least his occasions should require. Both my father and I made an exception against my uncle's letter and therefore stopped it a post; we represented to him the jealousy it might give our partners as then expressed but he said there was no harm in it. You will guess in the main the scope of the letter and what is meant by it, and it would not doe amiss if you should by word of mouth discourse the substance so as not to give offence.

You know every additional duty is a burden upon a trade and this lately laid on will contribute to make it go heavily this next year. This will make the dealors more absolutely necessary to us than otherwise, who must exert themselves in the Regulation and for that service only to make things go smoothly on; it is the only way to free us from general complaints which the last year had like to have brought us into troubles, which where they would have ended God knows. Should you quarrel with the dealors att this time, you may guess att the disturbance and interruption they would unanimously give to the trade. And though you were to engage all the other dealors in your interest, yet they are most of them people of little or no substance for which reason they can't force a trade; if they doe it must be by the creditt you give them and what sort of reckoning you will have with them att the making up your accounts you may judge. When an answer is given to the dealors it must be don with great caution, least if they be discarded their natural malice and spirit of revenge will readily prompt them to produce the letter and probably may bring us into trouble. For instance were it expressed that some of the Ten had received £50 for sale of Fieldhouse coals contrary to the stipulation of the law , if this letter were exposed, as certainly it would be by them if disobliged, the Review would lay hold of it and handle us as last year, that it was a plain proof of a designed monopoly; so that what now seems to sleep would be raised up against us and a
prosecution would certainly be set on foot. What then you will say can be don? We think a cautious letter to them must be framed, but particular instances of their false dealing should be represented to my uncle in a letter to him and that he may charge them with by word of mouth. I think it would not be improper if the general answer to the dealors be first enclosed to him that we may peruse and alter if thought necessary. Believe me we can't be too cautious as the world seems disposed. My father writes on this head to the Captain by this night's post, by the help of which the meaning of this may be explained where it wants. I doubt the proposal of paying £2000 att Michaelmas next and £1000 after will scarce go down, but when the 5 have come to a general result let it be dispatched as above. As to an interest for your own concerns att Gate, it is time it should be looked after and you must employ some friend of yours to transact for I must not appear nor can be of any service. It seems necessary Mr Ord must keep back his leadings whether we keep up our interest with dealors or not. The sexton's adventure made me smile and reflections upon it are such as I should guess att. I have now tired myself sufficiently and the more because this weather does indeed sensibly affect me who am ...

P.S. I desire you will send me an account of what money I advanced on the Bensham upper seam service. I remember not perfectly well now Brainslope concern was to be divided; as I take it I was to advance the charge of half that concern for the Captain's use as we agreed att Percivall's. If I be wrong set me to rights and direct your answer to this postscript enclosed to Mrs Clavering in Bedford Row. Adieu I am ...

I have often since the receipt of one of your letters some time since reflected upon the contents and now by experience find them true. There are some people in the world endeavouring to trip up my heels or rather to cut my throat with a feather, how justly I know not. I thought I might have deserved better att their hands when I formerly stood in steed of a father, but it is likely former kindnesses are effaced and forgot. It is with very great grief I must tell you that I am suspected, att least to me it seems so, of having raised a considerable sum out of the colliery more than was fitting for my own use and therefore I am refused a request of working 50 tenns for the supplying the quantity allotted me by the Regulation. A small favour demanded God knows to be rejected; and methinks the gain of about £2000 in twelve years service is no very extravagant allowance for one's service and pains, not to mention the entire ruin of a man's health, which att this time is a savage rent charge. But all this I am resolved to bear with patience. The lossess att Bensham are all attributed to my neglect; all losses by fitters or others in the way of trade in my time are not directly but by a side wind levelled in some measure att me. If I have bin guilty of any advantageous thing to the family, that is not noticed or looked upon to be an incumbent duty. My friend we live in an age of generosity; little did I expect such usage, but since I am deprived in effect of being a collier att home, I shall
take leave of trade and desire not to be concerned any way relating to it. My service has bin pernicious, therefore I will prevent it for the future; I desire if you have any thing to recommend or propose, let it be don directly by letter to my father. Then you may have an answer but I may sollicitt weeks without number before a resolution can be taken on which a certainty may be relied on. Witness this business of Fenham; I have formerly discoursed that point over and over, yet I believe you may have thought my answers very superficial because I could send you no other. Indeed my father is so ill now that he can't think of business, but depend upon it when he is better I durst venture a wager he will have so many objections that before they be answered a vast time will be spent. Therefore herafter when you have any thing to communicate do it directly to himself. Pray enclose your answer to this to Mrs Clavering in the Row under a cover and I conjure you not to signify the least of the above mentioned to any person living. I foresee in a little time as things are managed there will be great feuds among us, which I can't but bewail. Pardon the freedom I take but since it is to so particular a friend as yourself I venture to doe it.

My father is something better, returns you his thanks; he apprehends the length of the way, the trouble of securing way leaves through so many different proprietors and the uncertainty of the lease makes him wave thinking of it. Doe you think John Headword might not be willing to admit of a partner or two and let the colliery come down his way? You may if you think fit try his pulse, suppose Jimmy, you and myself should stand to a half. This I only recommend to your thoughts. To the rest of your letter I must give an answer when my father is in better plight and myself too, for what with these northerly winds and vexations of one sort or other I am almost off my legs. This day I received a letter from the 4 directed to Mr Edward Wortley and me desiring we will employ Nevill Ridley as a solicitor to watch the bill and receive instructions from us. Don't you think him so great a friend to Wrightson as to communicate anything we shall entrust him with to that gentleman and that Alderman Fenwick will be informed from time to time? Doubtless they will. Adieu my good friend and let me be in favour or out you shall always find me according to former professions ...
P.S. Was not the Captain to have had a share in Brainslope after won, as we agreed att Percivall's; was not I to be att a partcharge in winning and what might she cost? Your answer to these. I almost think it would be worth your while to come up on your own account to settle your own private concerns as well as those att the Gate for yourself. I shall be willing to contribute out of our joint concern att Bensham towards the charge and right glad should bee to see you.
26 June 14th 1711

I am favored with both yours. The latter was the most acceptable since it brought an account of your safe landing att Gateshead, though you had suffered in the journey by the loss of the Red Lyon juices, but as crabs and lobsters are so easily come
att with you I doubt not your speedy recruiting. I have drank the German spew water and you know writing makes it fly into the head, therefore must be short and so shall fall to business. Mrs Smith is uneasy till Mrs Barnes's business be concluded, she having obliged her friend to fit up an apartment for her on purpose. You will discourse Joseph and let that matter be made an end off one way or other speedily. Mrs Smith is a woman of experience and doubtless if she will be free in giving advice in any sort, she wants not capacity. We are both of opinion that the overplus sum remaining in the hands of your dear Peggy Ramsay belongs to herself, and should you contest it, Mrs Smith would comb your head for such a presumption were you within her reach. As the world goes I don't admire people's being called strictly to account. I think your vend is extraordinary considering how the season has bin for leading; if you can add 2 keels more to your number, it can't fail of doing well for there are no stocks att steaths, as the masters inform, even Clavering Stella was grounded. I believe you will find the trade grow worse every year after this therefore receive the advice you formerly gave to another person, make hay while the sun shine. Get what carriadge you can and lead what is possible; both ships and pans will swallow what ever are brought down. This day I was att Gate and see Captain Oldner, who told me the town was more than half supplied. He had sent up the river Lord William Powlett's coals this day. Price is Team from 25 1/2 to 26s , Hutton and Benwell 28s . My father desires cousin Baker, Bullock and Hutchinsons might take a view of Fenham, that their thoughts might be imparted to the Captain and yourself and that you would send him an account what steaths they might be brought to and about what charge; and if not to advantage but through Mr Montagu, by what means could that be compassed. You and the Captain must draw up a scheme and that will give us an insight. Bowman is here and presses an end of that lease to be made. I have not heard a syllable of the project of widening of our way but what yours mentions. I could not get a penny of money att the Gate this morning . Captain Oldner was wishing that he had had a list of the ships that loaded of your coals sent him, meaning that he would have bin serviceable to you. I am rather better than when you left me though not much; this hot and sultry weather is burdensome to me and were I not refreshed with some cool
breezes in the Bedford Row, I fancy I should cease to be. My father desires your acceptance of his best services and so does Mr Honywood who is by. Hugh has bin almost every day att the custom house without effect; he grows very peevish on it. I have wrote a letter and sent it to Lord William to sign to Sir Matthew Dudly, one of the commissioners, by which hope for some success. Did you borrow a blue coat from the master of the Gun Tavern and if you did, where was it left? Captain Oldner was making enquiry after it. Mrs Smith makes a tender of her devoirs to her beau, who she says writes such plain lines as she can't venture to read unless in a corner by herself. Pray pay my compliments to the cash keeper and the honest Alderman. I remain ...
P.S. When will they begin to lead from the new work att Whitefield Stella?
31 September 10th 1711

Methinks the time of my confinement very tedious, both as to the length of it (which is now near 5 weeks and may be as much longer for ought I know) as also being debarred the use of my penn, which was wont to be a diversion to me though perhaps a nuisance to those I corresponded with. However I would venture that with my friend, as I do att present to transgress my doctor's rules by stealing a few short lines in part answer to your last favour of the 28th ult. First then, I find that some people with you are masters of the secret off getting off bad coals in quantities, and it is certain that there has seldom come up more trash to a markett than by this last fleet. I freely own I could have wished that our Stella fitters had not bin so much
strangers to that mystery. I think their commodity was not inferior to the Black Burn or some others, which have disposed of a considerable quantity while our people stood with their arms cross and seemed like Solomon's sluggard; they apprehended a lyon to be upon your key, so durst not venture abroad to sollicitt. Strange perverseness in mankind. The distemper is visible and deeply rooted; we have sufficiently suffered this year but there it is not likely to end. Pray good friend turn your thoughts as my doctor does in the case of my body politic; when an application has bin once tried (which he hoped would have succeeded) and that failed, he rested not till he tried another. And as I have the greatest opinion of his physical performances, so I justly entertain the like of yours in this business. You are upon the spott and know the several parts of the trade that are affected and can give the best guess att the cause, and when that is known pray who can prescribe better. I must own I doe expect no redress but from your endeavours, yet even those can avail little unless the chiefs concerned, that is the 5, should cotton better together than att present they seem to doe; and doubtless the dealers are not unacquainted with the divisions and will improve them by setting distinguishing marks upon some particular concerns. As to the upper seams, spare no industry to get off in this last fleet, though att a less price; they will be infinitely worse for lying over year, increase your dead stock and ten to one but after Christmas 2 or 3 in the score will open the trade. I see no help for it. Sunderland grows upon us while we lessen, yet every Tine owner is not I suppose willing to abate one chalder of what his vend has bin for years bypassed and this must needs occasion strange distraction. Would it not be worth your while to postpone the raising of a trunk till we see what turn both the trade and the owners of that concern think to take? Charles Sanderson has bin out of town near a month and not yet returned, which occasions his silence in your regard; when I see him shall acquaint him etc. My father's offer of taking the tickett was with no other design than hopes of serving you without prejudicing himself. I paid uncle Robert the two £25 for the first payment . Mrs Smith has writ to sister Peggy which she says quits scores with you; sends her services, as I do mine also to her and the honest Alderman .

Kind friend, we are now busy furnishing our little house from
top to bottom; and let us contrive as well as we can, will cost us new beginning housekeepers a handsome sum of money, which will drain more than I am att present master off. And as you intimated in one of your former that you would remitt me some towards the latter end of the year, I desire it might be sometime next month if you can possibly , for it will be then that we shall enter upon our new quarters and I shall have several bills to discharge. I must further beg of you to watch John Linskill and desire him to deliver you for my use the bill of sale of a 1/16th part of his ship, which belongs to me and the man has never had the manners to do it as yet. If he be not in the ship, pray desire Frank Rudston to write to him for it was partly att your neighbour's instance that I adventured with him. Pray likewise acquaint honest Jimmy that considering the circumstances of our Stella trade, it seems absolutely necessary that we should have orders from the court how to proceed and then we act securely. To this end a state of the colliery as it is att present with all its difficulties must be drawn up and represented, as also a prospect of gift this next year; and of another hand if that colliery should not be carried on, the inconveniences that would ensue as first the decrease of rents for want of employment , the loss off the way which would in a manner be entire by rotting upon the ground, the certainty of steath rents etc. to which we are confined by lease. After this the court must judge what is fitting for us to doe and we must pursue the directions given, and then come on it what will, we shall be kept indemnified and blameless in the eye of the world. This must be thought of and returned me up so as to be presented this next term, so pray lay your heads together. I have no more to add, being in an uneasy posture with my 2 legs on a stool almost as highly elevated as my rump. I can't give you authority to drink any new health; I know nothing of the matter further than that the means is frequently made use off for obtaining the end. No more but due respects to friends in your neighbourhood ... P.S. My doctor has ordered me to drink punch in moderation, a pint a day. I want some good brandy; pray use your endeavours to procure me some and may disperse 3 or 4 bottles with one master and as many with another. Let them be sealed and tied down. You must also get my madam a table suit
of huckaback from Darlington, which I remember is very fine and good of the sort. Adieu. Harry Waters has some money in his hands of mine, £6 14s 6d, the balance of Tom Walker's profitt which you will receive for me and reimburse yourself for these commissions as far as will go.
33 October 4th 1711

I don't know if I am indebted to my kind friend or no but be that as it will it is no matter; I don't stand upon ceremony, which always ought to give way to business. And as this is the critical time for deciding the fate of the trade and on the resolutions taken depends welfare or ruin, I long to know what steps have bin taken on that head. I have repeatedly
recommended both to Jimmy and the Captain to have an understanding in this weighty matter and though either party should suffer a little, better so than the whole go to distraction. Two posts ago I had a letter from the latter, who gives me an account of his installation, thanks me for my thoughts of the renewal of the Regulation, which to him seem the most natural. He adds a computation of charges for laying a way from Urpeth to join our own way, as also those of working, and so draws it into a scheme of profit and loss. The quaerys I desire to be satisfied off are whether the lease is to commence att present or after old Tom Bewick's death; whether there be a possibility of obtaining way leaves through Kibblesworth grounds and through Ravensworth town fields where are so many different properties? The rent is easy enough. And Black Burn's wain trunk might be converted into a waggon on that occasion very conveniently. He leaves it to me to communicate to my father if I think proper. Accordingly I did in the gross; had I not, perhaps some exception might be taken which I will industriously avoid. I can't yet have his answer. But if the concern were actually taken, she would fall most naturally both for working and leading down Mr Headword's way, if he could be prevailed to be content with a share of her and contribute to part of the laying charges through his own ground. This would certainly turn to best account. But of that you can best judge and inform. This fleet is come up. Att their arrival coals were 26s 6d the best, but then the markett was att a stand and since that I hear it's occasioned by the Yarmouth men refusing to sell but att 29s. I must own I think them in the right. I have wrote to the Captain this post who will discourse you on the points above. I heard you were out of order; pray write particularly to the doctor or send it to me, for without particulars the doctor will not prescribe. I hope Mrs Ramsay (to whom my humble service) will oblige you; there is nothing like taking things in time. The youngest of Misses Clavering I doubt will scarce hold out 3 days with a violent feavor in her head; poor creature, she has no less than 9 blisters on att this time and is not sensible. If our doctor recovers her he may work miracles. Poor Mrs Smith has likewise bin much out of order for a week by past. She keeps a foot and is to begin to morrow to take some of our doctor's sweetmeats. Adieu I am ...
P.S. Just now the Signor is come in, who in his travels this day hears that our Council disapprove of the peace as proposed. How true this is time will discover.
37 November 10th 1711

Perhaps my longing desire of hearing frequently from you made me complain without a cause, but I can assure you yours directed to Mr Ashley both came safe and sooner by many hours than if addressed to our own habitation, since in the winter season the post does not deliver our letters till the next morning . I should in Signor's short postscript have advised you of the receipt of yours but he was hurrying me to save a penny so that in all probability I forgot. I have no objection to Johnson's coming, save that by his cunning he may give the dealers a great insight into the foible as the French call it of the coal trade, which they understand too much of already. In the next place you will see they will never treat with us for Stella without the praemiums for the year before as well as this last; both which will amount to above £200, and perhaps should this be granted I question whether they can doe us or at least will doe us any great service. This is my positive opinion before he arrives, which you will communicate to my good friend of Lamesly and let me know his if we ought to comply provided we have some assurances, which by the by will not be better performed than former ones. But when we have made trial, more cannot be don for the Infant. Our Bucksnook must be wrought to supply the markett with good coal , nay choice good, the beginning of the year or otherwise the laboring oar will lye dreadfully heavy upon us all the year and that can't be born. Pray therefore send us word if we can propose to work a quantity of right good for this ensuing year. I foresee that concern can't be supported but while the coals are extraordinary, Contract or none. Once a fortnight there ought constantly to be a clear pay att pits and in part for carriadge; the oppression is prodigious by longer delays and gives Weatherly and others an opportunity of feathering his nest. Recommend this heartily to our friend, who I am sorry is engaged in the black trade if the concern be from Tanfield side. I was sensible from your first
undertaking the waggon way you would meet with difficulties and crosses in abundance. There was such a confederated tribe of rogues nested together and each plaid into the other's hand, that I could but admire you could make that impression that has bin made. I believe you will find the same game playing in Richmondshire among the miners and the quondam agents. I am att a loss what to fix you for your pains and trouble; if it should be answerable to either, I know the sum would be very considerable. But att this distance must leave it to Jimmy and your self. You will see what the concern has saved by the alterations and accordingly proportion the reward. I am satisfied £150 is the least acknowledgment that can be made you by the public for your signal services this last year: were they as sensible of it as we that were eye witnesses, they would make it att least a brace. These are my thoughts and pray communicate them to the honest gentleman of Lamesly, who I know will press as much as possible this affair in your favour.

My father had last night a large account of the last meeting from the Captain . I have but barely read it over. His quaery to me was what character those fitters have that are appointed for Bensham. They are all set up for themselves since I left you, att least were not of my acquaintance, so was obliged to answer by silence. This good effect the Agreement will have, that I hope it will keep both fitters and dealers in a better decorum. Waters's impudence ought to be corrected by the united body. We hear that Biker Main coal is got: what is your opinion? If the coal be tolerable, that concern may be a thorn in our side and may encourage the fitters to keep up their heads. We leave all management of Stella to the honest Vaudois with your assistance and he may depend the dealers will never treat about that concern without the full satisfaction for the 2 last years. But you shall hear more of this shortly for my head and stomach are much disordered and increased by the badness of the weather. The enclosed is my uncle's account of the disposal of your tickett by which you will perceive he has paid me on your account £45 7s 4d for which you have creditt. Yesterday noon dyed old Mrs Blakiston of the gout in her stomach, which had bin there near a month before she sent for our honest doctor but he came too late. The Parliament is adjourned to the 27th. Next post my wife designs Jimmy a long epistle. Our young pupil has behaved himself not so civilly as he should
to his sister Lady Cowper, which has given great offence and makes me sick of my charge. Did you put on board Ableson the Captain's wine he presented me? Pray remember me kindly to my factoress. My wife and Mr Genuine present to you their respects and I remain ...
P.S. I hear by the by that Brummell pretends to lay his way in spite of mankind. My hearty respects to my honest Alderman.
38 November 23th 1711

Yours enclosed to Mr Ashly came to hand this minute and have sent it to my father to peruse and give him time to consider of it. Therefore am now answering off book, having an hour of leisure and free from company. You desire to know my thoughts of a certain concern but I must first tell you my father's. He you know is very difficult to enter upon any new project which is attended with a present considerable outlay. He is very cautious, which none can blame him for. He sent for me and asked my thoughts. I told him that if way leaves could be had upon tolerable terms and the colliery wrought on such as yours and the Captain's represented, I looked upon it as a concern that ought not to be slipped by any means. After a few days he repeated the question; I continued of the same mind. Well, says he, will you go shares? Yes sir, said I, my present opinion is such that I will venture 1/4, nay to share 1/3 if you please. You are welcome, said he. Not long after he produces the several charges of laying the way and working, which he looked upon as too small considerably as well as the rent too great. As to the first I agreed with him that to win and lay the way, £1160 would not doe it. To that of working I told him I
thought I could satisfy him to a nicety in that point, for among some of my papers I was sure of finding a project with the exact charges of Mr Headword's att the time that Alderman White had taken this, and should look out for it. He was delighted with this. I brought it to him. And where the Captain's computation makes £1 15s the ten of 22 waggons , the other made £1 13s the 42 fother of 7 bolls each, so that the waggon tenn would be near upon 50s working , drawing water etc. Well, says he, proceed and set down every article what you think may doe. Accordingly I promised I would doe it very liberally, so set down 20d a gate for carriage and twice a day made 3s 4d for man and horse, which was as much as his own waggon men could addle. I reckond the way longer by a good mile than Norbanks, however set down 18s a tenn while Mr Montagu paid but 12s, yet I would not be positive but that Montagu had but 20 waggons to the tenn. I charged 5s per tenn for all charges att steath, which is more than will doe it, perhaps pay the steathman and under-steathman's wages into the bargain. The way leaves, steath rents, viewers and all salaries I think £250 yearly, including satisfaction for the liberty of his steath and of the way from the Cowclose to the steath. £2000 for winning the colliery and laying the way and waggons . All these sums except the last I thought would each overdo; and allowing 16 1/2 chaldron making out and double coal att 11s, fittage, keel-owners' wages and dealers at 6d per chaldron , there would remain £600 neat upon 600 pitt tenns. The chief dispute with me was whether the way over Urpeth dean could be effected without casting the way so much to the east as that it would be of the utmost difficulty to bring the waggons up to Kibblesworth . As to the rent he was of opinion that 10s was full much. I told him that it was not above 7s for a wain tenn and I thought not att all unreasonable. All this he desired me to draw out in a scheme and send it the Captain which I did above a week ago, and on his answer he will take his final resolution. I would not be over forward in pressing and had rather that things could be brought to bear under the proposal than upon a trial to exceed, for that would make him exceeding uneasy. The next thing that makes the case disputable is the apprehension that it will lessen Team vend and that I doubt is but reasonable to expect. But of another hand I
represented that if these coals went unmixed, they might probably yield 11s 6d so consequently £250 more yearly profitt; if mixed with Team, would help off with many of his small workings. Caverley Bewick was with us this day and will wait till we receive the Captain's answer.

Just now our parcels of wine and ale came home safe. We drank all your healths att supper. The former is very good and the latter we hope, though a little down, will recover with time. The brandy is safe and extraordinary measure. My good friend will accept of my best thanks for his very kind remembrance. The huckaback 2 pieces of 16d and 14d are with us and well approved off; that of 10 1/2d came not to our hands. I have bin large and particular on the first article of this letter, which you will keep to yourself; if hear further shall be sure to advise. The dealers were with my father 3 days ago. They eat so heartily that poor Mrs Smith could not forbear lifting up her hands, yet would not conclude absolutely for Team the next year though my father proposed doing by them as Mr Wortley did for Hutton and Benwell . For Clavering Stella they would not engage for 2s 6d per chaldron if the coals were such as last summer. And if they were assured that they were never so good this next, they would not touch a coal of them unless first satisfied for the year 1710/1711. What ever you doe be sure not to work any but what is choice good and little of Coalburn, as Jimmy and you shall agree, for retrieving the lost reputation. I wish Johnson does not give us the slip, as I have advised the Vaudois. I have wearied my self and my head is confused, but yours is so clear that you will be able I hope to hammer out my meaning. Adieu then and rest assured that I am ...
P.S. My wife salutes you. My respects to the honest Alderman and Mrs Margaret .
44 March 25th 1712 past 7 att night

It is of a long standing that I am indebted to you and since you are pleased to allow me that liberty now and then, I doubt I shall be apt to call custom. Your account of the last election was the most entertaining of any I have met with. I find your interest helped to strengthen that of the church by which you have curried favour with the diocesan, and though our friend Jimmy Nicholson is now allowed to be a white boy, yet I think you stand fairer for preferment while most of your former acquaintance lye under a black censure; how reasonably I can't say but shall leave you to judge. My father being never desired to give the little interest he had, resolved between the two late candidates to stand neuter and leave every one to dispose of their votes as they thought most suitable to their inclinations, but it seems the doctrine is this, those that are not for us are against us. This interpretation I suppose is putt upon it and so he is deemed an enemy to the person elected and the interest that brought him in, by which you see how the cloud still hangs over his head while you are so happy as to enjoy the brightness of the sun in its full meridian. Long may it continue to you in that perfection and answerable to your deserts, still hoping that you will not entirely forget your quondam friends, though now in affliction. But I must drop this subject and proceed to another, which to me seems more material. I must tell you that I had the honour to dine with your honest Recorder att my father's last Friday, who entertained me with your nice management of his sister's concerns in protecting them against a certain person that formerly by force had got a good yard within them. We drank the champion's health but alas! I was mightily dejected when I heard from Charles that he was confined to his bed. He executed his commission by showing the letters wrote by your servant ; and as for your project of communicating to Mr Pitts, I could not but approve off it and the rather since I find Mr Gibson is so far led by your friend Jackson that he will receive no other impression than what he has from him, especially when so backed as by the insinuations and representations of another gentleman, who threatens publicly to tear up all waggon ways that cross a high way or
street and so putt the trade upon a level. I won't trouble with a repetition of particulars since I know Charles , who was an ear witness, has given you them att large. Only excuse my adding to your proposal to Sir John Clavering (for whom Robert Wright assured Mr Gibson that he would engage the baronet should let way leave through his grounds upon reasonable terms) that you insist that he grant liberty for a number of years certain, not for his own life, which considering how free he makes with it may not spin out the length of your lease, though you should not renew.

I have not seen nor heard from honest Calverley since my last to the Captain on that score; my father went about a fortnight since to wait upon him but mistook the coffee house that he frequents, so lost his labour. That concern of his is the only one unopened in all your river that I should covet to be engaged in. Pray how goes on Mr Headword's waggon way? Mr Genuine would inform what past twixt him and two of the dealers in relation to your concern. They will not undertake for a quantity and indeed there are so many of them in such mean circumstances that you would not desire they should. I doe believe these two are the best of that set but if they will not undertake, I don't see but that if the master undertook for himself, it would be the safest way. But Signor expects your further orders and a ship of the coals for a sample. I am summoned to meet Mr Freak all my father's. Therefore must conclude with hearty wishes for your speedy recovery and the continuance of a health so useful to all your friends. Adieu honest William , I remain ...
P.S. A peace very speedily is expected.
45 April 5th 1712

I think I must not begin a letter without acknowledging double obligations, but if you had such disturbing weather as we have had of late, you would guess by your own constitution how much a far weaker is influenced by it; and in such circumstances writing is not allowed. It has affected my father not a little, who had begun a letter to you two posts ago but not yet able to finish. Indeed what chiefly disturbed him was his anxious solicitude about poor Kitt Stockdale, who being att diner 3 or 4 days since att Tom Gibson's, was taken so ill with a sort of convulsion that they were obliged to send three people in a coach home with him to support him, and it was so late before he could be removed that the news of his illness came not to my father till near 9 a clock, when good Mrs Smith was detached. She sat up with him as long as she could, being obliged to return to give an account. I can assure you it was a melancholy one since she never expected to see him more. Poor man he lay in such agonys till the next day that he came to himself, that you would admire he should ever get abroad; however his heart was good, and with some cordials (whereof a bottle of your brandy was one) he was brought in a chair to Red Lyon Street day before yesterday where he began again to relapse, but God be thanked, though extremely weak he is got abroad again. You may imagine considering the dearness there is twixt the two brothers what a confusion my father was in, who gave due attendance to his own brother even to the last extremity. This he desired me to acquaint you with and hopes for your pardon to his silence till next post.

I gave the Captain a full account of what passed twixt honest Calverley and me the day after I received his and your letter, which doubt not he has communicated. Calverley promised that when ever he received any account from the north about Urpeth (the letting of which he did not in the least expect) that he would call upon me in his way to his brother Tom and give me an account, but I have not seen or heard from him since. The loss of poor Joseph Barnes is not easily to be repaired. My wife and I went last Sunday night to sup att Mrs Wait's, where we found poor Mrs Betty Barnes melancholy to a degree and not without reason. I sent your last enclosed immediately away to Charles Sanderson . It is a complete answer to such allegations as one would not admire to see Brumell subscribe too, but for a person of the other rank methinks tic unaccountable; but one plainly sees that he pins his faith upon some people's sleevs. Charles and I had talked over the matter in my parlour and I gave him such reasons for your conduct as I was capable off and convinced uncle Stockdale fully, who is a person that is as well heard by Thomas Gibson as any. But Jackson has laid such a foundation in his opinion as nothing but time and experience can root it out. Therefore I think you are to blame if you concern yourself further. You have don handsomely and friendlily by Mr Gibson ; if he will still be led by the nose, much good may doe him. He may smart att long run. I am sensible the weather must have distressed your vend, as also that a trunk though never so small would have bin of singular service. You are left to act as you think fit in relation to that, whose judgement all ways sways with me. Get a ship for a sample as soon as you can when the weather is dry; if the coals be roundy, I hope Signor Projector may be of service, and be sure not to send the worst. Mr Genuine has bin sadly plagued with your Newcastle carrier about a box Jimmy Clavering sent up before he came to town, directed to Mr William Cotesworth merchant in London . Signor sends a letter for the box, which was delivered with a demand of 16s after the rate of 3d per pound; the payment was offered if he would give an acquittance, but that being refused, the money was detained. Now you must know he wrote twice to you about it to know if his paying 3d per pound for a box so directed would not be to your prejudice and that you would discourse the carrier, but you never took the least notice, so that his back is up
and what adds to it is since he had like to have bin arrested for the money. He has wrote I suppose an angry letter to Jimmy per this post, I suppose on the same subject. Pray if this day's Medley come to your town, read it; you will think the time well spent. I have nothing to add further save my respects to the honest Alderman and all friends that wish me well. I am ...

I am entirely unfitt for this employ therefore must be short, especially since I write by stealth and I know of my doctor's being here, who will certainly catechise me if he finds the pen in my hand. What I wrote to the Captain last was by my father's directions and am sorry it should have given any offence. The chief objection he has a mind to have removed was about the validity of the lease let by Jackson to Sir John and Brummell , for as I take it he had let everything that was in his power, and if that stand good what will a new lease avail us? If it would answer the ends proposed he would be willing to contribute his share among the rest of our brethren, nay even for Bensham it self rather than fail. But we would be glad to be first satisfied what are each man's proportions and to have that objection as above cleared. In the next place as to Clavering Stella, we that transact have our hands tied up and can't act with safety but by order of court. I have consulted a great person on this head, who tells me that before we were called to account before the court, we were att liberty to act according to the best of our judgement , but now that we are before our Master nothing can be don with safety for the trustees but by an order. However I doubt not you might menage the matter well enough if you would indulge honest Jimmy a little, but I beg of you not to mention a syllable of this to any person. As to the charges that may accrue by endeavouring to stop the proceedings through what you took off Tom Shaftoe, as it was don by order of the 5 so it must and shall be repaid and that punctually too, though I were to do it out of my own pocket for our share of Clavering Stella . Don't take any thing by a wrong handle I
beseech you; that you should imagine that we should either call your judgement in question, or your integrity, is all wrong my good friend. I could heartily wish that my head and hands would allow me so much liberty of thought as formerly. I would convince you that we are the same as usual. But by the by let me advise you to state the case plainly and send us up the particulars in a letter to my father, after which you shall have I doubt not a satisfactory account to your mind. Now friend my doctor is come and Signor along with him; there is so much noise I can't tell what I write, excuse therefore all faults and believe me to be with a cordial sincerity and true affection ...
P.S. I have charged Charles this day with your complaints. Excuse faults.
49 July 3d 1712

Yours of the 27th ult. lies now before me. It came but to hand late on Monday evening so that I could not send to Mr Sanderson, but on Tuesday I wrote a line to him to entreat him to come to my house any time that day which suited most with his convenience and bring along with him your two letters of the date yours mentions. He returned for answer by word of mouth that he would wait on me; accordingly I stayed below stairs till after 10 att night, att which despaired of seeing him, but just as I was undressing for bed some body rattled att the door and it proved to be my gentleman. I buttoned on my cloths and down I went. I told him I had a budgett off complaints to produce against him for his slowness in proceeding in your business. I read to him part of yours. He told me that he had all along told you the reason of his delay was that he could not proceed till he had got Jackson's answer, a copy of which he had got out of court that very afternoon and not before, and that now he was prepared to go thorough stitch and apprise the court all att once; that as success hitherto constantly attended him, he did not doubt but in less than a fortnight's time to give you an account that would be to your satisfaction, and that he would shortly go to Sir Joseph Jekyll one of your council to give him full instructions and desired I would accompany him. I told him that if he thought I could be any ways serviceable, on notice I would attend. He showed me the 2 letters of the 26th April and the other. I explained it to him as I had don some time before so that he owned he thought himself perfectly master of it. Before our conversation ended it struck 11 a clock, which was the reason why I could not write by last post, and before we parted made him promise me he would write att large to you by this post and give you a particular account. As for the ship off Cliffton's I can't tell what will be don. Signor has bin twice down about him but can't get a coal off: they offer him but a guinea a chaldron . I went down on Tuesday last to the Gate where I see Captain Cliffton, who told me he had bin near a month att the markett. I inquired what praemium he had to give, the master; he told me 9d per Newcastle chaldron . If I mistake not, said I, Mr Cotesworth wrote me word he did allow you 12d. No indeed
sir, not one farthing more than 9d. Upon this I sent for Robert Watts and told him that he would oblige me if he would help off with that bulk of Bensham upper seams and should receive 4 1/2d per London chaldron provided he would give 22s, which was the lowest price that any of the 11s coals passed att. He would not engage further than a promise to help off with 3 or 4 score att the latter end off the ship. I then sent for Arlington, Hartley and Wren; promised them the same praemium but first of all desired the master not to mention whose coals they were, because you had a little difference with the two latter, but only should call his coals Bensham upper seames, which he did. They likewise promised a little assistance; as for the other dealers not one would touch a coal. In short the master does not I find understand the Gate and he will meet with much difficulty. I told him that I hoped to be down once more this week and then shall inquire how those that have promised doe perform, though I own I expect little from either the great or small dealers. I am going to make a visit to our honest Durham Recorder who leaves us to morrow. Wishing you all health and happiness concludes me ... P.S. I went down to the Temple where I see Charles who will give you a full account this post. He likes the affidavits wonderfully you gave him; was asking me if it would not be a prejudice to the lord's colliery if that waggon way was suffered. I told him that it would doubtless; for this reason, that the other coals were a much more vendible commodity which would be led down by that way att a much cheaper rate than usual and in vast quantities, and consequently must lessen the vend of those that had a meaner sort, much as the lord's lessees generally had, and so must throw up their leases etc. He told me it was a very material point and wished you could send up an affidavit to that effect which would be of very singular service. Adieu, excuse errors, I have not time to peruse.
52 August 26th 1712

Your very entertaining letter by yesterday's post has revived a little my low pulse, which any that feels it would fancy I was expiring. For this ten days past I have not bin able to set pen to paper but once to Jimmy Clavering , and that was a work of necessity that engaged me to give him an account of the insolent behaviour of those vile wretches att the Gate, who though they knew I was so ill as not to receive company yet forced themselves upon me. You will think it strange how they could doe so, but it was by a mistake in my man who told me they were some masters of ships who desired to speak with me, and accordingly were admitted. The first that offered himself was fat George Oldner , then his brother Richard , Blunkett and Coltman. We battl'd it for 3 hours till diner parted us: I neither offered them to eat nor drink with us. They insisted upon full pay but I
would not part with a farthing till I had Jimmy's order. I told them that they had almost every fleet bought Clavering Stella att 6d below the markett, and I could prove it upon them by several of our Team ships as well as others, and that Robinson's and Weatherley's coals which were bought for 10s got the same price with Clavering Stella generally speaking; that as they had not performed their part, I hope they would not blame me for keeping such a part of the praemium in hand to make satisfaction to our masters that were sufferers, etc. They stomached this extremely but I stood to my tackle. Indeed some expedient must be thought of to break into the measures of these great men, otherwise we shall be slaves with a witness, and this without loss of time. I am turning my head upon a project for Clavering Stella which considering the smallness of the quantity hope may succeed; it is among the petty dealers but where there is a quantity that will not doe. However I want such a headpiece as my friend William's to assist me or rather to correct my rude notions of trade, whose judgement I set no greater value upon than it deserves.

I congratulate you sincerely upon your late but signal victory but be sure not to trust to their honours . Charles is att Richmond, however I am preparing a note to your namesake the captain's son to dispatch yours away to his master. I am satisfied in conscience that what you have so earnestly and hazardously espoused and att long run carried, will prove the saving of the trade from ruin, nay beyond all retrieve, and doe you think or can anybody think it unreasonable that an answerable return be made you for your pains? I don't mean what was proposed formerly, because that was only for your friend and mine the honest Alderman but particularly appropriated to yourself. You have bin a considerable sufferer in your own private concerns to my knowledge and might have had terms such as you pleased to have insisted on from those you have now laid upon their backs, provided you would have given no obstruction to their destructive career. Sure then there is not a coal owner of any consideration in your river but that will make an offering to your self either in one respect or other that should be in some measure adequate to your sufferings and desert. Were I in the country, should be the first that should propose something of
this nature and shall in the mean time recommend it as far as I am capable. Considering that no real misfortune befell the judges, it was as lucky and pleasant a hit as could have befallen your antagonists. It is so remarkable that in an age it can't be forgot. You can't imagine how crest fallen are those mighty dealers upon these tidings. They used to threaten me with Bucks Nook, that the next year we should go a begging with our Team, Bensham and Clavering Stella for those and Hutton and Benwell would be able to supply the chief of the trade to this port with the best of commodity, and I should then plainly see the difference in price which should be 2s 6d per London chaldron . Oh this is a bitter pill to them. I must now beg excuse for breaking of abruptly. My head is sadly disturbed, and I wish I be able to write a few lines to my father; though have no novels of any sort, yet would not be wanting in paying my dutiful respects to him by inquiry after his health, now that the fatigue of the assizes is over. Howere least I have not time, desire you will plead my pardon. My best respects to all friends. I am ...

P.S. You must make excuses till next post to my father, for I am not in a condition to write. I see cousin Sanderson who promises to write to you but least he should fail, tells me that no affidavits can be preferred before next term. Adieu.
53 September 13th 1712

I had yours with the affidavit and enclosed answer to it in course. As luck would have it Charles Sanderson was come to town 2 or 3 days before, and happened to dine att my cosen's in Bedford Row that very day and was engaged to spend his afternoon there. Upon this notice I wrote a
note to him and dispatched it away. I told him that I had by that post received a packet with some matter of importance to be communicated to him, that I promised he should be dismissed in half an hour. Upon the receipt of mine the ladies who were att cards with him were very unwilling to part with him, but upon the promise that he should not be detained long they consented. I waited att home all the afternoon and about 8 a clock my gentleman made his appearance. I first produced the affidavit which he had seen before, then I read to him deliberately the answer to every particular of it, with which he was extremely pleased. I asked if any explanation was wanted, he told me no; that it was couched in such plain, easy and express terms that he could make your counsel as much masters of it as I was my self. He told me he had bin att the Lord Keeper's several times to inquire how matters stood, but he was in the country and not expected back for several weeks.
